utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you took earlier, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you a few questions this morning about your examination by Dr. Lopicic and some of the matters that you discussed with her. It appears from her report that when the interview began with Dr. Lopicic, you cleaned off the table and prepared the table for the interview; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If you mean in the detention unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And according to Dr. Lopicic, immediately after that -- I'm sorry. Immediately after she introduced herself and explained who she was and what she was doing, you began to describe to her your family history; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not right away. I don't know how we communicated during the conversation. If you mean that I started right away, we had our conversations for a day and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let me read the line in the report that I'm referring to. He she says, "After my introduction, he starts talking about himself and his family, about his events as well as about many years of his drinking problem." Am I correct in taking from that that you initiated much of the conversation regarding your family history and your drinking problem? It wasn't in response to specific questions from the doctor, you spoke freely about your background and history?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how I should put it. I don't know exactly how we started that conversation directly, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well let me ask you about the incident involving your belief that your mother committed suicide. You -- that was not in response to a question by her regarding the circumstances of your mother's death, that was something that you had -- you told her about, you volunteered that information; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in those conversations with the doctor as they proceeded, these life problems, how should I put it, and the situations that I had as a child and onwards and I told the doctor that my mother committed suicide. It's an assumption that that was so because to this very day, we don't know the cause of her death in order to be able to say exactly. And There is no grave. For anybody to be able to say that this and this is what happened, we to this day can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, it appears from the way of the report is written that the topic of your mother's possible suicide arose in the very first session that you had with the doctor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the first day, the first day of the talk. Perhaps the first hour or the first half an hour, I don't know exactly what time it was, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Okay. So I am correct in believing that it was first brought up by you within the first half hour or first hour of your discussions with the doctor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably that is true. Probably. I don't know the exact time, the hour, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, this was the first time you met Dr. Lopicic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know her before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, it also appears from the report, and correct me if I am wrong, that your aunt -- of the people who were aware of the possible suicide of your mother, two of those people were your aunt and uncle from Vardiste; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, my older aunts and uncles both on my mother's side and my father's side, they know and they never told us anything directly when we were children. I don't know. I remember my mother as if through a dream, but nobody ever emphasised this or told us about it. I think she had a nervous disorder. I feel very uncomfortable about speaking to this. I

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted], I don't feel comfortable talking about this. I really don't know what to say about this.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she took vinegar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since these are questions and since Mr. Vasiljevic began to talk about things that relate to his family and some people who are still alive today and they relate to illnesses in his family, I would request if it would be possible to discuss this at a private session so that Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic could respond to these questions in a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I suppose it's simpler to do it that way, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Will it take very long, this particular part of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, my cross-examination actually is going to be much shorter than I had given an estimate yesterday and it will -- all of it will involve these personal details so perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well then, we'll go into private session. Just one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are in public session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you described to Dr. Lopicic that when you began drinking or when drinking became a problem in 1984, that you would recall these events where, as you described it, you would talk nonsense; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1984, I believe that was the first time that I went to hospital in Uzice because of alcohol.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So I was already very deep into it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Around that period, did you begin to have different events in which you could not recall, but you believe that -- you could not recall exactly what you said but you believe that you had spoken nonsense? Did you say that to Dr. Lopicic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't remember, those were the 1980s. Before that, I would always know with whom I had been drinking and what cafes I had gone and how I had ended up at home, but in 1984 and 1985, no, even if I tried to remember, I needed more time to remember such details. And you know when I was in a cafe, I was always in a very good mood, I enjoyed telling jokes and I allowed other people to tell jokes about me. I was never bothered by that. I just wanted to have people laugh around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you learnt about some of the things that you said from the people you were with, that you had no recollection because you were drunk, but other people that were present told you some of the things that you said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would happen also, yes. I couldn't remember things. Sometimes if I -- if I had gone to three or four cafes, people would tell me where I had been. Sometimes I would remember, sometimes I wouldn't have any recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you characterised some of the things you said as nonsense and am I correct in believing that when you say nonsense, you mean things that were not true. You said things that were factually incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How shall I put it? Those things happened under the influence of alcohol but, you know, people tend to exaggerate also afterwards when they tell jokes about what had happened. People in cafes are mostly tipsy or drunk. It's not that we were ashamed, but you know, there were cafes where everybody was drunk.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, my question to you is: On these occasions when people told you some of the things you said, isn't it true that some of the things that you said were not true, they were factually incorrect; yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand you. If somebody told me what I had talked about, whether I denied it, whether that was true or not, I really don't quite understand what you mean with your question. Would you please repeat your question? I'm not sure I understand you correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You described to Dr. Lopicic that when you drink, as early as 1984, you would say nonsensical things, you would talk in nonsense. My question to you is: That -- what you're describing as nonsense, isn't it a fact that some of those things you said were untrue?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Many times people would tell jokes at my expense but they would also say things that were simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, isn't one of the other things that you told Dr. Lopicic is not only did you say nonsensical things you could not recall, but you also made promises to people that you never kept; isn't that also true? Didn't you also tell Dr. Lopicic that when you drink you make promises to people that you do not keep?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I would forget. If I promised something, sometimes I would forget. I remember promising once to a Muslim colleague of mine to go and do some work on his house. The following morning, the phone rang and I completely forgot what I had told him but then later on I would remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were such cases when I promised things and then completely forgot about them or, for example, people would ask me to pass a message to someone they knew in the village and I would forget that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, if you just answer the question, we'll on a lot more quickly. If there's something to add, Mr. Domazet will give you the opportunity of adding to it after the questions by Mr. Groome have finished. But you do tend to give us everything that you think should be said. Just answer the question to start with and Mr. Domazet can ask you to expand upon it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I want to now take to you April of 1992. In your discussions with Dr. Lopicic, you describe an event in which after you moved your family out of Visegrad, you went, and without your wife's knowledge, you took your daughter from school and brought her with you to see some relatives; is that correct? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And when you took your daughter from school, I believe you told Dr. Lopicic that your wife became so concerned that she contacted the police; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The child was supposed to be taken back from school and it was my mistake, I'm fully aware of that, I was not on time. I went to see a relative with my daughter and yes, yes, when I failed to notify my wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Were you drinking at the time?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you keep your daughter at the relative's house over night? Is that why your wife became so concerned, because you were there over night?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not over night. I didn't stay over night. I never thought about it. The child didn't come back home. I didn't go back home and it never occurred to me to inform my wife and so when she realised that the girl was not coming from school, she became upset. She called the hospital, the police, they informed everyone. They were afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did the police locate you where you were with your daughter?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, they didn't know where I had gone with my daughter. I'd gone to see a relative of mine who lived in an area two or three kilometres away from my place. Nobody asked any questions about it later on. Nobody knew me in that area. It's just that I didn't inform her.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I also see in the report that you said to Dr. Lopicic that towards the end of May that you had memory lapses, that there were events and things that occurred that you have forgotten. Did you say that to Dr. Lopicic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And those memory lapses, are they due to you drinking?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, partly, of course alcohol affected me but it is also the strange feeling that I had at those moments. I would be frightened, I would start talking. It was something that I had never experienced before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, given what you've told us about your cousin who was killed, there's very little detail about him in the report and I'm wondering, did you discuss at any great length your cousin with Dr. Lopicic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did. I don't know how much time we spent discussing it, but she did ask me about him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever tell her his name?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did. I don't know. I think I did. I don't know whether I told her his name. I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you describe for her how you felt or your reaction to his death? Did you describe that to Dr. Lopicic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, in the -- at some point, you and Dr. Lopicic talked about what happened on the 7th of June down by the Drina River and it appears, according to the report, that you told Dr. Lopicic that after Milan Lukic told the men to go down -- to get out of the car and go to the river, that you actually embraced Meho. Did you tell Dr. Lopicic that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Milan embraced Meho. She may have misunderstood me or maybe it's just a mistake in what she wrote about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I must say that's the word I read too, Mr. Groome. Have you got the page reference?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It's page 9, Your Honour, about the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So you -- you're saying that you did not say that to Dr. Lopicic. What you told her was that Milan Lukic embraced Meho?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that's what I said. Maybe she made a mistake when she wrote it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, with respect to what happened regarding the horse, according to the report, it appears that you told Dr. Lopicic that you rode past the hotel on the horse; is that correct? Did you tell that to Dr. Lopicic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was not quite clear. I told her about where I worked. I probably told her that I worked in the Panos restaurant, but I don't think that she correctly understood me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, my question to you is: When she says, "He passed by the hotel," did you tell Dr. Lopicic that on that horse, you passed by the hotel?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I told her the restaurant, not the hotel. I could not have said that. I am familiar with the restaurants of course and the hotel, so probably we spoke about the hotel where I used to work for a number of years, but I think maybe the doctor didn't put it down correctly. She did a lot of writing. She may have made a mistake. I could not have said in front of the hotel because I had not reached the hotel. I had already fallen down.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Aside from writing down notes, did she tape record her interview with you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think she did. Only if she had something in her bag, in her purse. She didn't tell me that it was being recorded at any rate. I may have said in the vicinity of the hotel, near the hotel. That is possible, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, I've reread page 9. Are you suggesting that we should interpret that particular statement that it was the accused who embraced Meho because it would then mean that we would also have to read it as having suggested that he, the accused, ordered them to go to the Drina and ordered to start the shooting at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was how I had originally read it last night, but I'm satisfied with his explanation that he was referring to Mr. Milan Lukic as he did at his testimony earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Perhaps you were working late at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I must say that I was surprised when you put the suggestion, and I am glad to say that to hear that my memory was correct, but I was going to interrupt you for another purpose, really. Mr. Domazet, do you know whether the doctor did record all of this? It's quite reasonable and frequently that doctors do this. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I don't know. Really, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I thought it might save a little time. I'm sorry then, Mr. Groome, I thought that might assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Also from the report, it appears that maybe it was the doctor's misimpression or something you said to the doctor that Zika Savic, the ambulance driver was one of those people that ran to your immediate assistance. Did you tell the doctor that Zika Savic was there when you fell off the horse and that he ran to your immediate assistance?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know how she phrased it. We discussed it for a while, for quite some time actually but he wasn't there at that moment. I don't know how the doctor phrased it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will read that particular sentence so you will know how she phrased it. "Some people ran to him, among them Zika Savic, the driver of the ambulance, and they took him to the hospital in Visegrad." That's how she phrased it. Did you say that to Dr. Lopicic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, that's not the way I put it. I told her what I had stated before the Court. I don't know on which -- on what information she based her conclusions, but I didn't say that I was next to Zika Savic at the very spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vasiljevic, I wanted to take you back to that interview that you, myself, and an investigator from the Office of the Prosecutor had in November of the year 2000 and you will recall that I had asked you at that time whether at the time of the river shooting on the 7th of June, whether you felt you were suffering from any psychiatric disorder or mental disorder and you said no. My question to you today is do you still stand by that answer or is it an answer you would like to change?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do I know? I mean to be perfectly frank, it's not something that I knew about at that time. I didn't know the right diagnosis and those feelings that I had, the impressions that I could talk to creatures and heavens over the phone, some saints or the devil himself. I don't know. I just remember being frightened, but it was all mixed up. It was a big confusion for me. I don't know. I don't know how to tell you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But all the symptoms that you are now describing, and you have described to Dr. Lopicic, they all occurred after you went into Uzice hospital; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I told her, I did have some kind of premonition -- no, that's not the right word. I -- it seemed to me that I knew things, that I knew that someone I know would be killed, but I didn't dare say it as if some higher power prohibited me from saying that. I don't know how to explain this to you. It's all very, very strange.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to the 7th of June. At that time, were you having premonitions from higher powers?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You mean in June? June and July?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm talking about the incident in --

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about June.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The day I'm talking about is the day Meho died. The day Meho died?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When I asked you earlier or a year ago, you said that you did not think you were suffering from any mental disorder on that day. It was after that day and my question to you today is do you still stand by that answer or do you wish to change it?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How -- I don't know how to put it. It was this fear that I experienced. I don't know how to explain this to you. It's not that it was all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm asking you do you want to change that answer; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even before that, I experienced -- I really don't know how to put it. I experienced such problems, some lapses like some void spaces. There was something in the air which made me feel uncomfortable and I had this feeling of -- this desolation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, we're not talking about feeling uncomfortable, we're not talking about feeling empty, we're talking about whether you believe you were suffering from a mental disorder on the 7th of June, the day Meho Zavic was killed. Do you feel you were suffering from a mental disorder on that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I was. It's -- I don't know how to express myself. Something did exist, but I cannot be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And a year ago, when you gave a very clear and unequivocal "no," that your mental problems began after that day and, in part, as a result of that day, when you gave that particular answer, were you not telling us the truth on that day?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe we didn't discuss the subject. I told you what I told you. I never thought that it would come to this. What I said, I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, according to Dr. Lopicic's report, it appears that -- or the first symptom that I can find in the report is after you were in Uzice hospital and my question -- and I'm sorry, and according to what you told Dr. Lopicic, it seems that those symptoms began to appear as your access to alcohol was restricted, when it became difficult for to you drink. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't drinking in the hospital for about 15 days or maybe it was just small quantities. It's not that I had any problem while I was abstaining from, for example, three days, and after those three days I would start eating again. As for what happened in hospital, I don't know what to tell you. I was afraid for my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vasiljevic, the symptoms you described to Dr. Lopicic, your thoughts about the birds outside, your thoughts about what you could do when you blinked, your conversations with other worldly entities, all of that occurred after you stopped, you began to abstain from alcohol; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Even before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, let's -- which symptoms did you experience prior to stopping the drinking in the hospital? Which of those symptoms did you have prior?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Blinking. Every time I would blink, somebody got killed, and if I thought that it was a child, I would feel terrible. I don't know who else I imagined I was talking to and then those telephone conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, let's just take blinking. When did you first believe that every time you blinked, somebody died?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know? I wasn't yet in hospital. Before that, I don't know exactly how long.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Are you saying that you had these thoughts prior to going into the hospital, that when you blinked, people died?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have these thoughts about blinking prior to the death of Meho Zavic?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did. I believe I had those ex -- experienced those things even before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And did you have those thoughts prior to the death of your cousin?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I did, but it happened gradually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So Mr. Vasiljevic, I would imagine we each blink two or three times a minute. Are you telling us that as from a period before your cousin's death up until the time that you received medicine, you believed every time you blinked, people died?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, not all the time. It's just that I would have this feeling all of a sudden. It sounds stupid, I know, because we all need to blink from time to time, but all of a sudden, I would just see this darkness around me. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of somebody who you believe you killed when you blinked?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it happened. Mostly it would be my children, that's what I was afraid of. It's all of a sudden somebody informed me that my child had died.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, are you saying that when I asked you that question a year ago about your mental health or your mental state of mind on the 7th of June, that even though at that time you believed when you blinked people died, you told me unequivocally that you did not feel that you were suffering from any mental disorder? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said what I said, but we didn't -- let me tell you, it was uncomfortable for me to speak about alcohol and all other mental problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, you spent quite an extended period of time in the psychiatric ward of Uzice hospital. You never told any of those doctors about this problem you had with blinking and killing people, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And you didn't tell any of these problems that you were having regarding the birds outside, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the birds, maybe they noticed something or when I would get out into the compound and -- when I saw a crow, for example, I would be afraid. I wasn't afraid of pigeons, but it was the crows that seemed malefic to me, ominous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: But my point is at the time you were being treated as an inpatient in the psychiatric facility, you never told your doctors about these two symptoms upon which Dr. Lopicic has based a rather significant finding. It was her that you told for the first time; is that correct? Yes or no, please.

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since my initial questions relate to members of his family that the accused has already talked about, I would like to request private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go back into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We are now back in public session.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Vasiljevic, in response to Mr. Groome's question whether these specific things about blinking and other things, whether you discussed that with doctors, you said no, and you answered him. My question is: Do you remember now at this point in time what you told the doctors at that time in 1992, what you told the psychiatrists in the hospital and what they asked you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not able to remember exactly what we talked about. I know only that once, the doctor who testified here said, "Oh, well, you've really calmed down, haven't you? What's the matter with you?" This was during the regular round.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is this something that you personally remember?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know this during one of the rounds after my treatment she had said, "Well, you've really calmed down. What is going on?"

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you remember the first few days during your treatment at the psychiatric ward? Do you remember what kind of questions were asked of you and what you told the doctors?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I was restrained. That's one thing that I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: As far as what you know about that illness and Mr. Groome's questions regarding that during that topic and that during the first interview, you said that you didn't have any mental disorders, were you aware, besides what you knew about treatment for alcoholism, were you aware that you had any other mental disorders?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know. They don't tell patients such things. There were more -- other patients there who had more serious disorders and they can't comprehend anything that would be told them about their disorder.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: One more thing about what happened to your mother. How much were the people who were around you, who were not members of your immediate family was known about her disorders?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, everybody in the village knew that. Nobody told us children anything about that, nobody from the neighbourhood, they felt sorry for us but everybody else knew more than we did. We were just kids.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And later, when you grew up, did anybody tell you anything more specific about this?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in the neighbourhood, nobody ever did. We knew what the problem was so nobody really told us anything about it. People felt sorry about that, but nobody ever insisted on talking about it. We knew that we knew a little bit about it. How much ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you assume why nobody talked to you about this subject with you and your brother?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody felt sorry about it. It's not comfortable for people to talk about illness. I wouldn't ask anybody questions about an illness myself to upset them, to upset a child.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: When you say a child, that was when you were little, but my question also relates to a later time. Were they also later evading this subject because when -- later when you were grown up, you could have understood these things in a different way?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I never really asked anybody much about it. Perhaps sometimes if somebody would tell me about it, yes, and they would usually tell me the best thing about it. And if anybody ever said anything about my mother, they would say she was a good woman. She worked. She was hard working. She liked to work a lot. But nobody ever said anything bad. Very few people would mention that she was ill. People would avoid saying that. Nobody wanted to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you think that anybody from your family would have any reason to be silent about this or to conceal this fact?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't concealed. It was common knowledge that we knew about this and how she disappeared, that she was missing. I know that as a child, everybody looked for her, my father's family, my mother's family. Many people from the village went to search for her for at least a month but they never found anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Except the people that you mentioned earlier, the people from your inner family circle, do you have information about anybody else suffering from similar conditions from your family?

utterances.speaker: MITAR VASILJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't have any information about that other than the people that I mentioned, two aunts, my niece, and my mother. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasiljevic. You can return to your usual place behind your counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Groome, we're very grateful to you for this anticipated schedule. You have somebody coming on Friday, I see and somebody on Monday and then some experts. First of all, are those expert reports provided yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This actually bears some explanation. I have some copies for the remainder of the bench. If I could pass those up and perhaps maybe work through the list and bring them to the Court's attention, a number of matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What I want to reiterate and I want to make this very clear that we have asked the Prosecution to fill in the time which is available until the Defence witnesses are available to continue with the Defence case. We're not expecting the Prosecution to complete its case in reply before the Defence case completes. It's purely a practical problem that we have already discussed so that whenever Mr. Domazet is able to get his two witnesses that he has outstanding along, we'll go back to deal with his case and then you can continue with your case. Insofar as anything happens during the continuation of the Defence case which arises -- gives rise to a matter in reply, you will be fully protected --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: -- in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps the best way for me is to work down through the witnesses. Mr. Selsky -- the witness is of such a nature I would think it would be appropriate that I make an offer of proof and have the Court make a ruling it whether it will permit me to call Investigator Selsky so with the Court's leave I will do that now and perhaps discuss whether the Court will permit me to call Investigator Selsky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, I just asked you, so that we're clear, when you say an offer of proof, you're going to show us his statement, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, there's no statement from Investigator Selsky. I'll just describe in a few sentences what I anticipate asking Investigator Selsky and see whether I will be permitted to call him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So You are just going to describe the nature of the evidence which you would hope that he could give.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I have to keep asking these questions because sometimes I think we speak a very different version of the language and I want to make sure that I have your terminology right. Yes, what would you anticipate he would say?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: What I would call Investigator Selsky to testify to, is Investigator Selsky is a investigator working on the case of Mr. Dragan Nikolic another indictee before this Tribunal. When Mr. Nikolic was arrested, he had two false identification papers of the Territorial Defence in his possession. During the interview of Mr. Nikolic, he was asked why he had these false identification papers and his explanation was as follows: That during the war it was very difficult for private citizens to obtain medical treatment and that he, as well as many others, obtained false documents purporting to be those of Territorial Defence members in order to permit him to obtain medical services when he required them on two different occasions. So that would be my offer of proof regarding Investigator Selsky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think there are two matters there. First of all, how does it relate to the Defence case that has not been raised already in the Prosecution case? And secondly, what does it establish against the accused?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would be introducing that evidence and arguing from it, Your Honour, that it is to show the unreliability of the records at Uzice. That it is quite possible that among other problems with those records, it was common for people to use false documents of Territorial Defence members in order to achieve or to receive medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the medical records, however, were tendered during the course of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm not offering -- I'm not purporting to tender any medical records through Investigator Selsky.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, no, the issue about the medical records and their reliability surely arose during the course of the Prosecution case in chief. They're Exhibits P136 and 137 or were they tendered during the Defence case? I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There were two pages of two of the records were tendered in the Prosecution's case, P136 and 137.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right. Well, then, how does this arise out of the Defence case?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: There was no -- this -- I can't imagine how this would have been relevant in the Prosecution's case in chief, this evidence. It arises because the accused now in the Defence case has alleged that -- introduced I think about seven or eight different ledgers purporting to be accurate records of all the people that were in Uzice hospital including the records pertaining to himself. I would be offering to rebut the reliability of those records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it must be the French translation I can hear going but it was -- they're obviously a long way to catch up and I'm sorry. Mr. Groome, you tendered documents showing his name in them that belonged to the Uzice hospital, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And not for the purpose of demonstrating that he was there, but for some other purpose, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, those records were seized as part of the Court order. They were introduced to -- in the sense of fairness and in the sense of completeness of the evidence in the case, it seemed appropriate for the Prosecution to put all of the relevant evidence that it should consider in this case before it. I made the decision to do that. I made the Court aware of this evidence in my opening and presented it in the case in chief because I felt, as an officer of the court under my duty and responsibilities as an attorney before the court to put all evidence even the evidence that may be -- that could be, or inferences could be drawn adverse to my case to put that before the Court. I did not take on the burden at that stage of proving the unreliability of the records that are maintained by Uzice hospital. It has been an issue raised on the Defence case and although this particular evidence is not directly on point, I believe it does -- it is relevant and does bear on the Court's consideration of what weight it should put on the total records that we -- that have been admitted in this case from Uzice hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can see the argument you make as to relevance, but you -- I am concerned, myself, to see where this arises as a case in reply. Now, if you tender the documents in chief, for whatever purpose, and you clearly were not doing it in order to prove that he was there. You were going to ask the Trial Chamber not to accept the accuracy of those records so that was an issue which arose during the Prosecution case in chief. That's so, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Perhaps the Court could assist me. When you say "issue" can you please perhaps define what it is -- can you articulate the issue that you see that I have raised during the Prosecution's evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The reliability of the two documents which you tendered because you were not putting them forward as being accurate because that would have destroyed your case in relation to the second incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I take from the Court's comments then that this -- the Court would have considered this relevant and admissible evidence on the case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. There is, of course, a lot of evidence about the unreliability of the records. One would expect hospital records to be unreliable from the way in which they are usually kept. Perhaps 40 years of hearing cases arising in medical negligence and the like, I've become a little cynical about hospital records, but there are many problems with these records not the least of which some of the people who were alleged to have been in hospital with the accused in Visegrad. But that is an issue which clearly arose at the time of the tender of Exhibits 136 and 137 and this material would have been relevant because you would have gone on to show that they were unreliable for various reasons, one of which is that people assumed false identities. But may I just ask you this question, and perhaps we're coming down to the reality of it. If the Prosecution case related only to the issue of when he arrived at the hospital, I don't know whether this is really relevant. If the Prosecution case is still he was never in the hospital, it is still relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I guess, Your Honour, as I view the case, the important fact is whether he was in the hospital at the time of the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, this is something I asked you some time ago when I had hoped that we would be able to dispense with a large number of witnesses and you told me then that it was still the Prosecution case that it was not the accused who was in the Uzice hospital because of the x-ray. Now, I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That has not changed Your Honour and I find it very curious that all the medical personnel that came here, at least the ones that I was present for, not one of them looked across the courtroom and said "That's the person I treated," or nor was there any other kind of identification procedure to draw the connection between the hospital record and the actual person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: A number of witnesses actually said that they would not be able to recall what he looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But two of them gave evidence of having known him personally as the waiter, and I think that rather ties it in. There's been no suggestion anywhere in the case that there were two waiters in Visegrad called Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I've endeavored to do on behalf of the Prosecution is to show that there are a number of indications that these records are not reliable. Whether that unreliability means that Mr. Vasiljevic was never there or was there at a different time period, or perhaps was there under a different name, I will not be able to offer the Court a clear explanation. There is no definitive explanation that I can glean from the evidence. I believe there is sufficient evidence and will be arguing that there is sufficient evidence, that records taken in totality are unreliable and should not be relied upon by the Court in making a determination that Mr. Vasiljevic was not present at the house fire.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The next problem, of course, is that what you are offering is not Mr. Nikolic to come along to say that he got these things falsely but to have hearsay evidence that that's what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, my next point on that is because it is a rather tangential issue, if Mr. Domazet does not agree to the evidence in the way that I wish to present it, I would endeavour to speak with Mr. Morrison and to explore the possibility of having Mr. Nikolic available in the new year for cross-examination and direct testimony on this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, well that may be the answer to that particular problem but my own problem at the moment and I'll ask Mr. Domazet what his view is, is that you are seeking to raise in reply something which was relevant in chief and which was raised in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I operated on a good faith basis that this was the most appropriate place to seek to introduce this evidence. I would ask, it seems that the Court and myself have maybe different experience in this. I would ask an opportunity to maybe do some research and to submit written papers on -- or some written argument regarding where such evidence may be most appropriate as I am unfamiliar with some of the positions the Court is informing me of now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There has been, if I may say so, a great deal of laxity in some of the earlier cases in this Tribunal where they had an almost completely new case in reply and then they had a case in rebuttal or rejoinder I think it was at that stage, and surrebuttal or surrejoinder and so on it went on. But I did make it very clear and I've made it very clear during several times in this case that evidence in reply must be strictly evidence in reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It would be my position that until the Defence introduced evidence that he was not present at the time of the crime, that there really was nothing to reply to. The fact that I chose to introduce the totality of the evidence that had been gathered by the Prosecution and to put all of that evidence before the Court, it would be my position until I have an opportunity to further research it, that that should not in and of itself be a bar to replying to the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we'll come back to it at 11.30. But Mr. Domazet, I will ask you what your attitude there is. There are two ways of looking at it. One is that it is not strictly evidence in reply and would require leave to reopen the Prosecution case to call it. That may be one way around it. The other is that it is of such tangential importance in the case that it shouldn't be, that leave should not be granted. But nevertheless, we'll come back to it at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet, what is your attitude first of all as to whether it is properly in reply and secondly, is there any reason why the Prosecution shouldn't be able to reopen their case to prove it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the examination of the witness, I did not notice, Your Honour, that there was any challenge as to the way he was -- as to the way the members of the Territorial Defence were admitted into hospital, at least as regards Uzice. If I understand my learned colleague, Mr. Groome correctly, the investigator who was not the investigator of this case because I don't remember seeing his name or hearing his name from any of these witnesses, I don't see that there was any testimony that the accused Nikolic had two forged identity cards of the Territorial Defence, that that was the reason for medical treatment. Whether that was the reason on behalf of Mr. Nikolic, I never noticed that that was any -- that that constituted a problem for admission of patients who very often came to the hospital without any medical documentation. I personally don't see any relevance of this information if that's what the investigator is supposed to testify about; however, should the Court find that it does have any relevance, let him be examined. But personally, I don't see any reason why that should be included in the case in reply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, it hasn't been tendered on the basis of that any reference has been made to Mr. Nikolic before or to this investigator. It is an attempt by the Prosecution to demonstrate that the medical records would be unsafe because of a practice about which Mr. Nikolic apparently spoke of people obtaining forged identity cards of Territorial Defence members in order to get medical attention easily. Now, what you say would be material going to its weight and you would be able to see whether you can cross-examine that or to -- you can point to other material that has been said in the case, not all of it uncontradicted but nevertheless it has been said that everybody got medical attention whatever their ethnicity and even without medical records. That doesn't make it irrelevant, though. It remains relevant. You can attack its weight as much as you wish. My concern was a technical one, but you say, as I understand it, if we believe it has some relevance, we make no judgement about its weight, but if it's relevant, you won't object to the investigator being called. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just that, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well -- just sit down for a moment, would you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Groome, we can see that there is some basis for arguing its relevance and on that basis, we will permit you to call the investigator. I think more properly, it should be as part of your case in chief, but that probably doesn't matter very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If I can maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But we're making no decision on its weight, that's a different matter altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Then with respect to the voice experts, the Court asked me earlier had that report been filed, and it had been filed several weeks. I had spoken to Mr. Domazet earlier today. He does wish to cross-examine the people involved in the preparation of that report. If I can explain to the Court, there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of the witnesses because I have not seen this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I will have somebody get the report, a copy of the report for the Bench now. The two people that were involved in the analysis of the audio tape were a Dutch examiner, a forensic examiner, and because it was in a different language, he sought the assistance of a linguistic expert in Serbo-Croatian language. So I would have both -- I'm attempting to have both of them available. I have not gotten definitive word on their schedules yet. We are -- I should have word in the near hour or two. We are attempting to secure their attendance for next Monday and Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So it's the Dutchman and the one who speaks B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They are the two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The report was filed on the 23rd of November and I can give the Court the name of the Dutch expert, his name is Dr. Broeders. The name of the assistant, the linguistic assistant, is not included in the report and she is actually requesting some protective measures so -- she's concerned about her identity being revealed publicly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean a pseudonym and facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: At least a pseudonym. I will inquire about the facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well, now, Mr. Domazet, have you any problem about the timing of them being called next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I received the report from the Prosecution, I believe, on the 22nd of November or thereabouts. I have examined the report. The only problem I have with it is that I was not in a position, being here, to identify any of my experts to examine the tape because I haven't received the disputed tape yet, that is the tape which is purported to carry the voice of (redacted). I have tapes of the interview given by (redacted) to Yves Roy in Sarajevo which was used for the purposes of comparison. However, as for the second tape which is being challenged here, and in respect of which the (redacted) (redacted) stated that it was not his voice, I have only the transcript of some portions of the tape but not the tape itself. If I can reserve my right for later on, if I can obtain the tape and then carry my -- conduct my examination subsequently, I would not have any problems with examining the witness, the expert in question on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, this has been the problem throughout. You are never in a position to cross-examine because you say you haven't got an expert report. Now, you are entitled to complain if you have not been given access to the tape and because it's still within the 21 days, by the time you get to the 10th, you have the right to object to it. But we are not going to have this done piecemeal, a bit here and a bit there. Are you going to get a local expert to have a look at it or are you going to have to go back to Belgrade to do it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I would request that this tape be given to me, a copy of this tape be given to me so that I can have it examined, but I don't have anything against this witness, Dr. Broeders, if I understand it correctly, to be examined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I wonder whether I'm getting through. I hope I am. Your obligation in cross-examination is to put to a witness your case. So far, you haven't done it because, as you say, you've never had a report. For example, Dr. De Grave should have been cross-examined upon what your expert was going to say and you didn't cross-examine him because you didn't -- you hadn't organised your own expert which means now the Prosecution has got a case in reply. This is not the way litigation should be conducted. I see little, if any, point in you not having an expert report when these witnesses are called because you will then subsequently call them and the Prosecution will have to bring back either their experts or some other experts in a case in surrejoinder or surrebuttal, I've forgotten which it is, and this is just not going to happen. Now, if you say you haven't been given the tape or a copy of the tape, that is unfortunate and it will be sufficient, I'm afraid, to say that we won't be able to hear these witnesses next week. Why hasn't a copy of the tape been given to Mr. Domazet, Mr. Groome?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just clear up a few things for the record. The day that I received this report, because of the unusual circumstances regarding this tape, I both notified Mr. Domazet and the legal officer of the Court, the very day I received the report, and I made all of this information available to Mr. Domazet. I asked him to coordinate with the case manager whatever he needed. He was given transcripts, he was given at least some of the tapes. I cannot tell the Court now why Mr. Domazet doesn't have that tape. I know it was made available to him back in the beginning of October when I received the report. The report is dated October 9th so that's when the report was first given to the Defence and the Court's legal officer was made aware of this unusual set of circumstances.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He told me it was the 22nd of November he was given it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's when I filed the report, Your Honour, but I think Mr. Domazet will -- I think he will admit and his memory will be refreshed because I had a specific meeting with him on this very unusual set of circumstances and I also told him that I would be advising the Court's legal officer because of the unusual issues raised by this. All of that information was available from October 9th onward. If it's an oversight on the Prosecution's part, I apologise. I think Mr. Domazet will also confirm that all this evidence has been available at any request. Had Mr. Domazet told us on the 10th of October or the 11th of October, "I got all the copies of the tape but the one I need," that would have been corrected back then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Unfortunately, though, I have to point out to you that Rule 94 bis requires it to be filed not less than 21 days and there is a decision of the Appeals Chamber, I've forgotten in which case, which has read that very strictly indeed. In fact, I would have thought, with all due respect to them, too strictly. But we are bound by that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I recognise that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That is very unfortunate. Especially as this is third time it seems to have happened that Mr. Domazet's not prepared to cross-examine somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was also -- my belief that given Mr. -- this witness's admission, I'm trying to be careful of what I say because this was also in protected -- in a private session. Because of this witness's admission to the actual meeting, to the conversation, to a lot of the topics raised in that conversation, it was my belief that until he said, "That is not me," it would not have been my attention to have sought the introduction of that tape or the introduction of that expert report and I believe it was filed either the very day or the very next day after that witness said, "That's not me."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I can understand why you haven't filed it but I'm concerned that we are bound by a decision which has read this as some sort of derogation from a party's right to have live oral witnesses being called without expert reports being filed. However, if there's any way around it, I mean -- I don't know when it can be done, but if a copy of the tape can be provided to Mr. Domazet, he may be able to have somebody look at it before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have a copy furnished to Mr. Domazet immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I would hope, if I may say so, that Mr. Domazet would not take a technical point of two days in the light of the unfortunate history of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: It would be my understanding -- if his experts wish to listen to the original, I will make immediate arrangements for the original to be shipped or sent in some secure method to whatever expert nominated by Mr. Domazet. I would imagine they would want to see the original tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There was some mention made at the time that this tape was played that it had been a filtered copy to get rid of background noise or something. Which one is it that the experts have to listen to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I would think that would be a question to be answered by the experts nominated by the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: My reason for raising it is do you think you can give both?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So there can't be any further delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Certainly. I would just ask for the original to remain in our custody until an expert is nominated. We will send it to them by some secure means so that they have the original. I will furnish Mr. Domazet with a copy of the tape today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, the comparison was with an interview with the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Nobody sent them the tape of his voice here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, although I have asked for a copy of that but I have no intention or plans to have any further analysis done at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet, it may mean that you'll have to do an awful lot of work on the telephone, but if this can be done in time for you to deal with them at least on Tuesday, it would be of great assistance to us. I can't imagine that their evidence would take more than a day between the two of them, would it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Your Honour. I've been rather generous with my estimates of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Domazet, you owe a small debt that you are required to discharge by doing something as rapidly as possible, if I may put it in that way because we have been frustrated by the absence of your experts in so many ways that this time, I think we should ask you to really pull out all stops. You're going to have, I should think, the whole of this afternoon and the whole of tomorrow to organise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I understand it correctly, you expect me to have the results by Monday, the results of my expertise of these tapes, expert examination of these tapes so that the witness can be -- the witnesses can be cross-examined on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I said Tuesday, actually, but I think Monday might be pushing it too far. But if you can get them organised and the tapes are sent, and you can get a report by fax, you should be in a position to cross-examine them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can try; however, I really don't believe that such an expert analysis can be conducted by then and that the results can be obtained by Monday. I don't really think it's possible, but I said, bearing in mind everything that you've said, and that we should not delay the proceedings any further, that the witness could be heard on Monday or Tuesday as was envisaged by Mr. Groome. I asked for the tape to be given to me because my idea was to conduct an expert analysis of the tape since, as far as I understand the analysis so far, it is possible that that was the voice of Witness [redacted]. Therefore, we do not still have a firm conclusion that it was indeed his voice. In view of all other evidence, I do not ascribe such importance to this analysis to these results as the way think stand now. Things may change after the examination of the witness, agree. However, once again let me state that it is true that I discussed the matter with Mr. Groome and that he had told me, I believe it was in October, that there was a report which, however, did not establish with certainty that that indeed was the witness's voice. And Mr. Groome told me that one more analysis would be conducted before he finally decides to use that as evidence. Since Witness VG81 did not raise this issue, this was not raised during her examination, I didn't think that this would indeed appear as evidence before the Court. So it was only on the 22nd that I received it, that I really examined it, but at that time I still didn't know that it would be tendered into evidence. So that is perhaps one more explanation concerning our conversations regarding this piece of evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I just clear something up there. As I told you, I have not seen it or if I have, I have not read it. Did you say that the expert's report so far only raises this to the stage of possibility, that it is possible that it was the particular witness's voice? That's as far as it goes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, what's that going to do for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I believe the way it's order worded is that the voices are consistent, it's the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Consistent, that only means possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Well, they're not different people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They're not inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Based on the limitations of the technique that was used, they cannot say beyond a scientific certainty that it's the same person but it would be the position of the Prosecution that the fact that the expert analysis reveals that they are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They can't exclude, that's what they're saying, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's right. And coupled with the witness's admissions about having the conversation, coupled now with the testimony of the person who was present there during the conversation, that taken all together, the Court would be entitled to infer from all that evidence that was the same person who made that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: So then the purpose of calling VG81 is to prove the circumstances in which the tape-recording was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Because she didn't deal with it in her evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: This is the thing that was raised on the first day of the -- first week of the trial. You made some reference to a tape at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Or Mr. Domazet did. It now starts to fall into place. Well, then, you will say that it's admissible simply through VG81's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And the weight to be given to it depends on the expert reports, but not the admissibility of the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The admissibility would not depend upon the expert report. The admissibility would be solely dependent upon the witness. The weight, however, would depend both on the expert report, his admission that the conversation took place and her testimony that "That is the same voice, that's a person I know and that's the tape-recording that I made of him."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that gives me a very different impression of what it's all about. If the expert says simply that he can't exclude it, that they are consistent but he can't say anything more than that, the cross-examination of him would not prove to be of such importance that you would need a case in reply, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Not in reply but whatever it is, the old terminology I thought went out with the passing of the Judicature Act in 1861, but they still survive in the Tribunal here, I see. The surrebuttal case, so that if Mr. Domazet is unable to cross-examine them based upon a report, but then calls his own experts assuming that they come to a different conclusion, you're not in any way prejudiced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet, thank you for that. That puts a very different complexion upon the situation. May I suggest, however, that you do your best to get an expert's report so that you can cross-examine this witness, but there doesn't seem to be the same problem about bringing witnesses backwards and forwards as we have, for example, in relation to the x-ray. But I hope that you will approach your attempts to get an expert to look at it in time with more enthusiasm than you expressed here in court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That was not meant to be a criticism, that was just perhaps an unfortunately-worded aside. All right, then. Well then, we can call those witnesses but I suggest that we do it on the Tuesday, Mr. Groome, to give Mr. Domazet the opportunity, but please make sure that he gets a copy at least of the principal one and that the originals of both the original and the filtered versions are sent to the expert nominated. I hope not through the Tribunal's mail system because that sometimes takes weeks to get to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And just if I can just remind the Court of my initial comment. These witnesses haven't committed, we haven't had -- confirmed their availability. We are making our best efforts to do that. We have confirmed with VG81. She will be leaving her home on the Saturday and will be here on Monday to testify. Now that we have moved those witnesses to the Tuesday, would the Court wish me to move Investigator Selsky to Monday and have a complete day Monday or still have two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, if you wish. We are obviously not going to be able to fill it up with anything else and we may as well not break up our time here too much. We're very grateful to you, Mr. Groome, and I know that we have been critical of you at times, but we're very grateful for you trying to fill in the time caused by the absence of the Defence witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, there are a few other matters that I would like to ask you. Going through all the evidence of the witnesses as to the times when events took place, it is very hazy in places, understandably, because they didn't have watches when the building was being burnt down. But a number of them talk about dusk. Now, this was the week before the summer solstice and if it was up here, I can tell you it was probably not dusk until about 10.00 at night, but I have no idea what it is was in this area we're interested in here, on the eastern side of Bosnia. So is there any way of obtaining any details as to when the sun sets on those -- I suppose both parties have an equal interest in this so I'm not terribly concerned how it's done, but if we can get some agreement as to when sun set was. There's been some evidence that it was raining in the afternoon. Whether that affected when sun set would have been seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, as the Court knows, in preparation for this trial, we attempted to do that and from all the international records that we could find, there was no location that was even close enough that I thought would have any reliability for the Court. If Mr. Domazet -- maybe there would be local -- more local records, witness information. I know in my own country there will be such records. I will furnish the material that we were able to gather on this and perhaps if both are put before the Court, the Court can decide which data will be more reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Domazet, I'm sorry, I'm just waiting for the translation. It is probably more in your interest than the Prosecution's interest to get the times sorted out, but I am a little concerned that we are left without anything other than sheer guess work at some of the times and references to dusk about the best that we get for some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What's the nearest city closest to Visegrad that would have some meteorological records?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we're talking about Serbia, then it's probably Cacak which is a little further away than Uzice or Kragujevac which is still further away. If we're talking about Serbia, as far as information that we can obtain, there is a Hydro-Meteorological Institute of Serbia which is responsible for providing information of this kind to the courts, and they do have this information and can provide such information. I can tell you that probably that we can agree with the Prosecution regarding this information and we can obtain this information in relation to the western countries such as the Netherlands. It gets darker in that period at least an hour or an hour and a half than it does here so the sun rises an hour to an hour and a half earlier. So this is seven or eight days before summer solstice and I know that in my town, dusk is at around 8.00 p.m., that's when it gets dark. I think that it really gets dark sometime between 8.00 and 9.00 p.m., and I think that that would also be valid for this particular period, so I think that we can make an attempt to obtain all this information and to get a uniform position regarding this particular statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The distance between Visegrad and Uzice was an hour and 20 minutes' drive an according to the doctor and an hour according to the ambulance and I think somebody gave us an estimate of the distance. I don't know in which direction it is and how far it would throw out any records they have, but there may be some way of assessing the difference between Uzice, that's the place that you're thinking of, and Visegrad. We'd get some -- at least a better idea than we've got at the moment. Well, can I leave that to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, in relation to your psychiatric report, it has a number of an annexes which are in Cyrillic, I don't know how important they are, but if even Dr. Moljevic has trouble reading Cyrillic, you can imagine the trouble we'd have. So if you can get an English translation, that will be of some assistance to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will do so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Groome, I'm sorry, you're on your feet already is there something you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I just wanted to finish a few comments on the planned reply case just to give the Court some additional information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just before you go back to that, can I just deal with two matters?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
